title: Refusal to bend, condemned
core: All of these describe someone who will not yield — will not change position, take advice, or be moved by pressure. What unites them is not the immovability but the **verdict**: each one is the disapproving name for a firmness that admiring words (*resolute*, *steadfast*, *tenacious*, *determined*) would praise. They split on what exactly is being resisted — an argument, a plea for mercy, an offer of terms, a hand on the wheel — and on who is doing the complaining.
exam_note: The GRE's favourite move is the neutral-vs-condemning swap: the passage supplies approval (*resolute*, *tenacious*), so the answer is the praising twin, not **obstinate** or **pertinacious** — read the surrounding attitude, not the behaviour.

words.nuance: The group's default and its plainest verdict: the digging-in itself has become unreasonable, with no further diagnosis of why. It names a **temperament** rather than a stance in any particular negotiation, and it is the cold, formal cousin of *stubborn* — strip out the affection *stubborn* can carry and you have obstinate.

The only one where the thing refused is **mercy**. Others resist arguments; the obdurate resist tears — pleading, pity, remorse bounce off. Moral, near-biblical, and reserved for the creditor who won't forgive the debt or the sinner who won't repent; using it convicts the person, not just their position.

The complaint is **duration**, not hardness. This is *tenacious* grip held an hour too long — the person won't drop the subject, the creditor keeps writing, the rumour won't die. It draws a sigh of fatigue rather than moral outrage, and it's the most bookish word here.

Stubbornness **at the bargaining table** — terms were offered and refused. It presumes a negotiation exists (talks, unions, parties, coalitions), so it describes a position taken, not a personality. It's also the one that can flip admiring: an intransigent defender of principle.

The opposite failure from the rest: not refusing to move but refusing to be **steered**. Plenty of motion, no listening — charging ahead on your own judgement while everyone shouts from behind. Usually aimed at the young and spirited, and it keeps a flicker of grudging admiration none of the others allow.

The blame word, and the only one that attaches to a single **act** as well as a person: *willful blindness*, *willful destruction of evidence* — you didn't slip, you chose. Where *intentional* is a neutral report of a mental state, willful is an accusation, and even in its headstrong sense it is never praise.
